also: take good care of your health
I hope you feel better soon

evidence: Cic. Fam. 7.15.2, closing a letter (Lewis & Short s.v. cūrō)
Traupman 19: take care (of yourself), tē cūrā
terms.comment: Lewis & Short gives sē cūrāre, to look after oneself, refresh oneself (Ter. Ad. 5.1.1; Cic. Phil. 9.3.6), but not as a leave-taking, which is Cūrā ut valeās.

terms.gloss: get well (said to someone who is ill)
evidence: Cic. Fam. 16.10: Fac, plānē ut valeās.
terms.comment: Cicero’s letters to his sick secretary Tiro end again and again with Cūrā ut valeās or Fac ut valeās: to someone who is ill the farewell means “get well”.

phrases.latin: «Cūrā ut valeās, mī fīlī,» inquit avia.
phrases.english: “Take care of yourself, my son,” said Grandma.
phrases.source: Libellus VI, Reditus: per Alpēs domum

phrases.english: Take good care of your health!

phrases.latin: Cūrā igitur nihil aliud nisi ut valeās; cētera ego cūrābō.
phrases.english: So think of nothing but getting well; I’ll see to everything else.

phrases.latin: Sed cōnfīdō, sī dīligentiam, quam īnstituistī, adhibueris, cito tē firmum fore.
phrases.english: But I’m sure that if you keep up the care you have begun, you’ll soon be strong again.

phrases.latin: Cūrā ut valeās, mī fīlī; crās lūdēmus.
phrases.english: Get well soon, my boy; we’ll play tomorrow.

sources: Lewis & Short: valeo
John C. Traupman, Conversational Latin for Oral Proficiency, pp. 16–17, 19, 94, 287.
